memory_leads.lead: Container equipment is a capacity pool distinct from vessel slots: a carrier can have nominal ship capacity yet be unable to accept cargo in a location because the right empty boxes are unavailable or not ready.

Container lessors form a parallel asset-ownership layer beside carrier-owned fleets, using operating/master-lease style arrangements and on-hire/off-hire transitions to shift equipment supply without changing vessel ownership.

Equipment on-hire/off-hire commonly carries condition, location and acceptance-state consequences, so a leased box changes economic availability through a handover process rather than merely through contract start/end dates.

Container depots are operational nodes for empty storage, release/return, inspection, cleaning and repair; depot capacity and gate throughput can therefore constrain usable equipment away from the marine terminal.

Interchange records such as equipment-condition/release receipts create a custody-and-condition boundary when a box changes hands among carrier, depot, trucker or customer, supporting later damage and responsibility allocation.

Maintenance-and-repair workflow has its own inspect-estimate-authorize-repair-ready states; a physically present container may remain commercially unavailable while repair approval, parts or workshop capacity are pending.

Periodic safety/fitness status and structural condition create an equipment compliance lifecycle separate from routine cosmetic repair; exact inspection standards, intervals and thresholds are deferred.

Reefer containers require a readiness chain beyond an empty dry box, including refrigeration-unit condition, pre-trip checking, power availability and temperature-control handoff; reefer-box scarcity can bind cold-chain bookings even when vessel slots exist.

Chassis availability can form a separate inland bottleneck where containers cannot be efficiently picked up or delivered despite terminal and vessel capacity; ownership/pooling models vary and exact jurisdictional arrangements are deferred.

Equipment-release and pickup instructions connect booking/customer demand to a specific available box and depot/terminal location; release validity, location and readiness make equipment allocation an operational state rather than a fleet-total statistic.

Trade imbalance creates directional empty-box deficits and surpluses, forcing empty repositioning by sea and inland moves; repositioning consumes slots, handling, storage and cash without carrying paying cargo.

Detention/demurrage-style time charges can function partly as equipment-circulation incentives and allocation mechanisms as well as revenue/penalty items; exact tariff definitions and legal treatment vary and are deferred.
Equipment procurement/disposal, lease extension, off-hire and repair-versus-scrap decisions create a box-level asset lifecycle whose timing can diverge from the vessel orderbook and fleet cycle.

The atlas effective-versus-nominal-capacity concept should include equipment-position availability: vessel TEU, berth productivity and inland transport can all be adequate while local empty-box scarcity still prevents shipment.

Port/inland congestion can amplify itself through equipment-cycle time: slow customer return, terminal dwell, depot queues and chassis shortages keep boxes away from export origins and extend the same disruption beyond the quay.

Liner capital intensity includes a movable equipment fleet in addition to ships and terminal interests; lease-versus-own decisions can alter cash commitments and flexibility without changing deployed vessel capacity.

Container tracking/event information refines known-time replay because physical location, release, interchange and repair-ready states may be recorded at different times from when commercial planners can reliably act on them.

The broad point that containerization reorganized ports, inland transport and inventory is already explicit in the atlas; P017 retains only the equipment-pool mechanisms that make that system operational.
The generic statement that ports and inland links can become the binding shipping constraint is already covered; P017 only decomposes one container-equipment channel of that constraint.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Blind recall is too salience- and geography-biased for an exhaustive lessor/depot/provider history.
Exact lease pricing, durations, fleet sizes and transaction economics require dated Evidence.
Chassis ownership, depot practice, liability and interchange rules vary by country/port and period and require Evidence.
Exact dimensions, inspection thresholds, reefer procedures and current regulatory requirements are outside blind-memory authority.

stop_reason: The movable-equipment lifecycle is populated from ownership/leasing through release, interchange, depot/M&R, reefer/chassis readiness and empty repositioning; further recall would become provider-, lease-rate-, equipment-specification-, country- or current-rule-specific.

method_observation.observation: For container shipping, effective capacity should be replayed as several coupled inventories—vessel slots, usable boxes by type/location, chassis/inland interfaces and depot/repair readiness—because a local shortage in any one pool can reject bookings without changing nominal TEU supply.

truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no lessor fleet, lease term/rate, depot rule, chassis regime, equipment specification, tariff definition or historical event is verified.
